title: After Callais, Baltimore is the blueprint
summary: The Supreme Court's Callais decision gutted the Voting Rights Act, but the court does not get the last word on the subject, write Avril Rayo and Luis Villa-Guzman, who say that history shows that the answer may not be back in the courts, but in the community.
content:
by Avril Rayo and Luis Villa-Guzman, Maryland Matters July 18, 2026

by Avril Rayo and Luis Villa-Guzman, Maryland Matters July 18, 2026

The April 29 decision from the U.S. Supreme Court in Callais v. Louisiana will change who holds power in this country. It does not erase the Voting Rights Act of 1965, but it cuts out one of its last working protections. This has been building for years through Shelby County v. Holder and Brnovich v. Democratic National Committee.

But this moment is different. The direction is now clear. The courts are not where this fight will be decided.

Justice Samuel Alito, writing for the majority, leans on Thornburg v. Gingles and flips it. What used to be a pathway to challenge discriminatory maps is now a dead end. Section 2, the core protection against racial gerrymandering, is effectively gone. As Ruth Bader Ginsburg warned, it’s “throwing away your umbrella in a rainstorm because you are not getting wet.” That is not a metaphor anymore. That is where we are.

Section 2 was the tool people actually used. It was how communities proved their votes were being diluted. That tool is now out of reach. States have more room to redraw districts with fewer limits. Lines can be drawn to split Black and Latino communities and weaken their voice. On paper, the maps may look neutral. In practice, they are not.

And this shows up in who holds power. The Congressional Black Caucus could lose between 13 and 16 members. That is close to a third. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus could lose up to five seats, including four in Texas and one in Florida. Representation does not move in one direction. It can expand. It can also contract.

But the impact does not stop at elections. If race cannot be considered even to fix discrimination, the logic spreads. Housing. Education. Jobs. Budgets follow power, and power follows representation. When representation shrinks, so does investment. So does access. That shift does not happen overnight, but over time it reshapes entire communities and limits future opportunity.

So the question becomes simple. If the courts step back, what fills the gap? Baltimore answers that.

In 1910, Baltimore passed the first racial zoning law in the country. Black residents were barred from majority-white blocks. When those laws were struck down, segregation did not disappear. It shifted. Restrictive covenants took hold. Then in Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), the Court barred enforcement of those covenants. It was a legal win. But it did not dismantle segregation. It exposed something deeper. The law alone does not reset power.

That gap is where organizing begins.

In Baltimore, Black communities did not wait. They built infrastructure. The Afro-American newspaper, founded in 1892, became a hub for action. By the 1930s and 1940s, it reached over 200,000 readers. It reported on discrimination, but it also mobilized people. And it was not alone. Baltimore had more than 30 Black newspapers. That is not just media. That is a network.

Churches played the same role. Bethel AME. Sharp Street Memorial. These were not just places of worship. They were organizing centers. They registered voters. They planned campaigns. They raised money. They sustained momentum.

Leadership came from within. Dr. Lillie May Carroll Jackson built one of the most disciplined NAACP operations in the country. Thurgood Marshall developed legal strategies from Baltimore cases that later reshaped the nation. The courts did not lead that work. They responded to it.

That is the throughline. When the courts narrowed protection, Black communities in Baltimore widened organization. That pattern is consistent. Scale. Density. Duration. Coordination. Civic infrastructure did not follow the law. It pushed it. Over time, that pressure led to changes like the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

After Callais, we are back in that same position. The courts are narrower. Protections are weaker. States hold more power. The law is not going to move first. It never has. People do.

Baltimore did not wait for permission. It built institutions. It built leadership. It built pressure. And then the law followed.  That is the blueprint now.
